title: Implement a gRPC logging interceptor, a rate-limiter interceptor, and a bidirectional streaming service (live stock prices).
shortTitle: Implement a gRPC logging interceptor, a rate-limiter interceptor, and a bidirectional streaming service (live stock prices).

s1_definition.profdef: A gRPC logging interceptor is a `ServerInterceptor` that wraps every call to log the method, latency, and final status, giving uniform observability without touching business logic. A rate-limiter interceptor is a `ServerInterceptor` that counts calls per client (often with a token bucket) and rejects excess traffic with `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`. A bidirectional streaming RPC declares `stream` on both the request and response, so the client and server exchange messages continuously over a single long-lived HTTP/2 stream, implemented by returning a `StreamObserver` whose `onNext` reacts to each incoming message.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture National Bank of India's trading floor. The logging interceptor is the CCTV that records every order that comes through with a timestamp and outcome, so nobody has to add cameras to each desk. The rate-limiter interceptor is the doorman who allows only so many orders per second from one trader so one greedy client cannot flood the exchange gateway. The bidirectional stream is the open phone line between a trader and the live price desk: the trader keeps naming stocks they care about, and the desk keeps shouting back new prices, both talking at once on the same call until either hangs up.
s1_definition.oneliner: Logging and rate-limiter interceptors are cross-cutting ServerInterceptors, while a bidi stream declares stream on both sides and uses a StreamObserver to send and receive continuously on one call.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A gRPC logging interceptor is a `ServerInterceptor` that wraps every call to log the method, latency, and final status, giving uniform observability without touching business logic. A rate-limiter interceptor is a `ServerInterceptor` that counts calls per client (often with a token bucket) and rejects excess traffic with `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`. A bidirectional streaming RPC declares `stream` on both the request and response, so the client and server exchange messages continuously over a single long-lived HTTP/2 stream, implemented by returning a `StreamObserver` whose `onNext` reacts to each incoming message.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture National Bank of India's trading floor. The logging interceptor is the CCTV that records every order that comes through with a timestamp and outcome, so nobody has to add cameras to each desk. The rate-limiter interceptor is the doorman who allows only so many orders per second from one trader so one greedy client cannot flood the exchange gateway. The bidirectional stream is the open phone line between a trader and the live price desk: the trader keeps naming stocks they care about, and the desk keeps shouting back new prices, both talking at once on the same call until either hangs up.

**One line to remember:** Logging and rate-limiter interceptors are cross-cutting ServerInterceptors, while a bidi stream declares stream on both sides and uses a StreamObserver to send and receive continuously on one call.

sections.s2_technical:
A `ServerInterceptor` implements `interceptCall(ServerCall, Metadata, ServerCallHandler)`. For logging, I wrap the `ServerCall` with a `SimpleForwardingServerCall` so I can observe the status in `close`, record the start time, and log method and latency when the call ends. For example `long start = System.nanoTime();` then in the overridden `close` I log the method name, the status code, and the elapsed milliseconds, which gives one consistent log line for every RPC.

A rate-limiter interceptor keeps a counter or token bucket keyed by client identity, often taken from a metadata key or the peer address. On each call I try to acquire a token; if none is available I `call.close(Status.RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED.withDescription("rate limit"), new Metadata())` and return an empty listener, otherwise I delegate to `next.startCall`. A simple approach uses Guava's `RateLimiter` per client, for example `limiter.tryAcquire()`; a more precise approach uses a sliding window in Redis for a distributed fleet so the limit is shared across instances.

Bidirectional streaming is declared in the proto as `rpc StreamPrices (stream PriceRequest) returns (stream PriceUpdate)`. The generated server method signature returns a `StreamObserver<PriceRequest>` and is handed a `StreamObserver<PriceUpdate>` to push responses. The pattern is that I create and return an inbound observer whose `onNext` handles each subscription message from the client, and separately I push price updates to the response observer whenever the market ticks. Both directions run independently over the same HTTP/2 stream, which is why gRPC can do true full-duplex that HTTP/1.1 cannot. A senior nuance is backpressure and lifecycle: I should respect flow control (the generated `ServerCallStreamObserver` exposes `isReady` and `setOnReadyHandler`) so a slow client does not cause unbounded buffering, and I must call `responseObserver.onCompleted()` or `onError` to end the stream cleanly, and stop the ticker when the client disconnects to avoid leaks.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's trading desk needs one consistent record of every gRPC order call with its latency and outcome, and bolting logging into each method is error-prone and inconsistent. This is exactly what a logging interceptor solves — one place logs every call uniformly.

Problem 2 — One aggressive algo-trading client can hammer the price gateway and starve everyone else. This is exactly what a rate-limiter interceptor solves — it caps calls per client and rejects the excess with RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED.

Problem 3 — Traders want a live, two-way feed: they keep adding symbols they care about, and the server keeps streaming fresh prices, all on one connection. This is exactly what a bidirectional streaming RPC solves — both sides send messages continuously over one HTTP/2 stream.

The demo shows a prices proto with a bidi RPC, a `LoggingInterceptor`, a `RateLimiterInterceptor`, a `PriceStreamServiceImpl` that streams live prices, and a `PriceClient` that subscribes to symbols and prints updates. Classes and steps: `prices.proto`, `LoggingInterceptor`, `RateLimiterInterceptor`, `PriceStreamServiceImpl`, `PriceServer`, `PriceClient`.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build (protobuf plugin generates streaming stubs)
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run server
java -cp target/classes com.bank.prices.PriceServer

# Run client (subscribes to RELIANCE and TCS, prints live prices for 3 seconds)
java -cp target/classes com.bank.prices.PriceClient

# Trigger the rate limiter: fire more than 5 calls quickly from one host → RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a trader opens a live price stream and subscribes to RELIANCE and TCS.

Step 1 — The client opens the bidi stream. The LoggingInterceptor records the start time and the method name, and the RateLimiterInterceptor checks this client has not exceeded five calls; if it had, the call would be closed with RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED.

Step 2 — The client sends two PriceRequest messages with action SUBSCRIBE for RELIANCE and TCS on the same stream. The server's inbound StreamObserver.onNext adds both symbols to the subscribed set.

Step 3 — Meanwhile the server's scheduled ticker fires every second, checks the stream isReady for backpressure, and pushes a fresh PriceUpdate for each subscribed symbol back to the client over the same HTTP/2 stream.

Step 4 — The client's response observer prints each update. After three seconds the client calls onCompleted, the server cancels the ticker so there is no leak, closes its side, and the LoggingInterceptor logs the method, final status, and total latency.

```
2026-10-26 15:15:01 [INFO] gRPC START bank.PriceStreamService/StreamPrices
2026-10-26 15:15:01 [INFO] SUBSCRIBE RELIANCE
2026-10-26 15:15:01 [INFO] SUBSCRIBE TCS
2026-10-26 15:15:02 [INFO] RELIANCE = Rs.2456
2026-10-26 15:15:02 [INFO] TCS = Rs.2431
2026-10-26 15:15:04 [INFO] gRPC END   bank.PriceStreamService/StreamPrices status=OK 3012ms
```

```
  │    WHY: stack cross-cutting concerns in order, reusable        │

  ── State: Bidi Stream Lifecycle ──────────────────────────────
  [OPEN] ──SUBSCRIBE──→ [STREAMING] ──onCompleted/onError──→ [CLOSED]
      │                     │ ticker pushes updates             │

  1. client opens StreamPrices (bidi)
  2.   → LoggingInterceptor.start  → RateLimiterInterceptor.acquire

```
sections.s6_takeaway:
This question is really three things that fit together in a trading-platform gRPC service. The logging interceptor and the rate-limiter interceptor are both server interceptors, which is gRPC's mechanism for cross-cutting concerns, and the live price feed is a bidirectional streaming RPC. For the logging interceptor I implement interceptCall, record the start time and method name, and wrap the server call so that when it closes I log the method, the final status code, and the elapsed milliseconds. That gives me one uniform log line for every single RPC without adding a single line of logging into the business methods.

For the rate limiter I keep a per-client token bucket, keyed by the remote address or an identity in the metadata, and on each call I try to take a token. If none is available I close the call with RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED and return an empty listener so the call never reaches the service. In a single instance a Guava RateLimiter or an atomic counter works, but across a fleet I use a sliding window in Redis so the limit is shared, otherwise each instance would allow the full quota.

The live stock prices feature is a bidirectional streaming RPC, which I declare in the proto by putting stream on both the request and the response. The generated server method hands me a response observer to push updates and asks me to return an inbound observer. The trader keeps sending subscribe and unsubscribe messages on the same call, and a scheduled ticker keeps pushing fresh prices for the subscribed symbols, both directions running independently on one HTTP/2 stream. This true full-duplex is exactly what HTTP/1.1 cannot do.

In my banking work at National Bank of India the trading desk used this design so traders got a live two-way price feed, every order was logged uniformly for audit, and one aggressive algo client could not flood the gateway. The senior details I always mention are backpressure and lifecycle: I check isReady on the stream observer before pushing so a slow client does not cause unbounded buffering, and I cancel the ticker when the client disconnects or completes, because a streaming server that forgets to stop its background work leaks threads and memory very quickly in production.
